What each test establishes

All three comparisons · Repeating hidden variation, heavy density 2.25
TestA · HzB · HzB − A · centsResult
Halves308.600377308.6003770.000000Same pitch
Quarters678.435281678.4352810.000000Same pitch
Extra eighths1173.3333331760.000000701.955001Different pitch

The halves and right-hand quarters are Ptolemy’s comparisons. The eighths are our extra diagnostic. The uniform profile passes all three. Heavy outer quarters give matching halves but unequal right-hand quarters. A repeating mirrored pattern passes both ancient comparisons, but fails the extra eighths test. A heavy left half fails the first comparison while its light right-hand quarters agree.

Uniform segment: frequency = (1 / 2 length) × √(tension / mass per length).

Nonuniform segments require the wave equation through their actual mass distribution. This model uses eight piecewise-constant cells, ideal fixed boundaries and constant tension. A 110 or 220 Hz completely uniform full string sets the modern reference. It does not assign an ancient absolute pitch. The wave equation, mass profiles and additional eighths test are modern teaching choices. String stiffness, damping, bridge width, support compliance and changes of tension caused by a real bridge are omitted.

Equal pitch here means numerical agreement within 1e-7 cents, a computational tolerance rather than a human hearing threshold. Reflected mass distributions have matching spectra. Passing a finite set of comparisons cannot establish arbitrary material uniformity.

Read the examination

Ptolemy, Harmonics I.8, selected phrases from John Wallis’s Greek text and Latin translation (Oxford, 1682), pp. 35, 37–38. These are excerpts, not a continuous chapter translation. Greek ligatures and Unicode are normalized; segment letters are capitalized instead of barred lowercase. Latin long-s is normalized; & is retained. English translations and grammar notes are new.

1 · First, halve the whole

Πρῶτον μὲν ἐπὶ τὴν γινομένην τοῦ ὅλου μήκους διχοτομίαν

Primo quidem, ad factam totius longitudinis bisectionem

First, at the bisection of the whole length

An excerpt from the construction instruction. διχοτομίαν / bisectionem means division into two. τοῦ ὅλου μήκους / totius longitudinis is ‘of the whole length’: the genitive names what is being divided. The midpoint is Κ in Greek and K in Wallis’s Latin diagram. Printed p. 37.

2 · Then halve the half

καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν τῆς ἡμισείας διχοτομίαν

deinde, ad semissis bisectionem

and at the bisection of the half

Another construction excerpt. The half from Κ to Η is divided at Λ. The two new parts are quarters of the whole string. ἡμισείας / semissis means ‘of the half’. These are the source’s second comparison, rather than a second comparison of the original halves. Printed p. 37.

3 · Equal in pitch?

τὸ ΕΚ τῆς χορδῆς μέρος, ἰσότονον εὑρίσκηται τῷ ΚΗ· καὶ ἔτι τὸ ΚΛ, τῷ ΛΗ

si chordae pars EK comperiatur ipsi KG aequitona; & KL, ipsi LG

if the string’s part ΕΚ is found equal in pitch to ΚΗ, and also ΚΛ to ΛΗ

Selected condition, not a complete sentence. ἰσότονον / aequitona means ‘equal in pitch’; it does not mean ‘equal in physical tension’. The print uses barred lowercase segment letters, normalized here to capitals. Greek Η (eta) corresponds to Wallis’s Latin G, and Λ to L. The text continues by treating the string’s constitution as unvarying; the modern counterexample below explores the limit of that inference. Printed p. 37.

4 · When the trial fails

Ἐὰν δὲ μή· μεταφέρωμεν τὴν δοκιμασίαν ἐπ’ ἄλλο μέρος, ἤτοι χορδίῳ ἄλλῳ

sin minus; transferendam esse probationem ad aliam chordae partem, aut etiam ad chordam aliam

But if not, let us transfer the trial to another part, or to another string

An excerpt of the instruction following failure. ἐὰν δὲ μή / sin minus means ‘but if not’. μεταφέρωμεν is a ‘let us’ subjunctive; δοκιμασίαν / probationem is the trial or examination. Wallis casts the instruction as ‘the trial is to be transferred’. The instruction gives a concrete response to a failed instrument check. Printed p. 37.

5 · What must stay comparable

τὸ ἐν τοῖς ὁμοίοις καὶ ἀναλόγοις καὶ ἰσομήκεσι καὶ μίαν ἔχουσι τάσιν, ὁμότονον

ut in similibus, proportionalibus, longitudine aequalibus, eandemque tensionem habentibus, sit tonus correspondens

sameness of pitch in like, corresponding, equal-length parts under one tension

The Greek clause crosses from p. 37 to p. 38. ἰσομήκεσι / longitudine aequalibus concerns equal lengths. μίαν ἔχουσι τάσιν / eandem tensionem habentibus concerns a single tension. ὁμότονον concerns pitch. Those are three different conditions. Our model fixes length and tension and varies mass per unit length. Printed p. 38.

6 · An instrument for testing

Κανὼν ἁρμονικός

Canon Harmonicus

Harmonic canon

The heading of the instrument diagram on p. 35. κανών can mean a straight rod, rule or measuring instrument. The diagram is part of Wallis’s 1682 edition, not an ancient blueprint. His long note on p. 36 discusses and changes the drawn bridge surfaces; the complete pages retain that editorial evidence. Printed p. 35.

Three reading checks

The two halves agree. What follows?
These two measured pitches agree; try the quarters too. A mirrored mass profile gives the halves the same spectrum even when neither half is uniform.
What does ἰσότονον mean in this trial?
Equal in pitch. Ptolemy names pitch, length and tension separately. Agreement in one quantity does not establish the others.
The repeating profile passes both ancient comparisons. What does the eighths test show?
These two comparisons can miss a smaller pattern of variation. Eighths are our additional diagnostic. This chosen repeating profile is a counterexample to proving uniformity from only these two equal-pitch comparisons.

Reopen this experiment · Complete scanned edition · Derivation and source decisions.

Ptolemy’s instrument examination precedes his use of string divisions to test concords. The selected wording treats the string’s constitution as unvarying after agreement. The repeating modern example makes the limit of that inference explicit. Wallis discusses and changes the bridge drawing in his note on p. 36; the full scans retain it. No claim is made about the precision of a physical ancient instrument.
